derivation: For one forward transaction with no page moves and no continued writes after savepoint/statement rollback or SQLite error, pInJournal prevents a second main-journal record for an original page. Newly appended pages above dbOrigSize have no original-page record.
Each record occupies page_size+8 bytes: page number, original page, checksum.

Charge one initial header, one possible initial CACHEMOD spill, and one later new-header sync for each newly journalled original page: N+2 headers. After sync all NEED_SYNC flags clear and state is DBMOD; later new pages alone do not set NEED_SYNC.
Charge 65536 bytes for every header and 65536 more for its preceding alignment. This uses the pager maximum, without assuming the usual Linux sector size.
Maximum conditional content is N*(page_size+8)+2*65536*(N+2). The existing copy-layout model additionally rounds content and charges one entry plus one inode allowance.

The page-move error path can clear pInJournal and repeat a page. The planner rejects both auto-vacuum header fields and additionally requires complete caller/native-VFS review proving no page moves, ATTACH, VACUUM, setting changes or transaction retries before any writer admission. Savepoint/statement rollback followed by further writes is also excluded: the N+2 header argument assumes the single forward NEED_SYNC/CACHEMOD-to-DBMOD path.

The input requires rollback-format read/write versions 1, exact current header/physical page count, absent journal and absent/zero WAL/SHM. Full independently hashed source identity is rechecked after the bounded descriptor header read.
excluded: statement journals and all SQL sorter/materialization scratch
continuous peak or complete original journal bytes
continued writes after savepoint/statement rollback or SQLite error

commit-no-new-header.text:
/* Write the super-journal name into the journal file. If a
      ** super-journal file name has already been written to the journal file,
      ** or if zSuper is NULL (no super-journal), then this call is a no-op.
      */
      rc = writeSuperJournal(pPager, zSuper);
      if( rc!=SQLITE_OK ) goto commit_phase_one_exit;

      /* Sync the journal file and write all dirty pages to the database.
      ** If the atomic-update optimization is being used, this sync will not
      ** create the journal file or perform any real IO.
      **
      ** Because the change-counter page was just modified, unless the
      ** atomic-update optimization is used it is almost certain that the
      ** journal requires a sync here. However, in locking_mode=exclusive
      ** on a system under memory pressure it is just possible that this is
      ** not the case. In this case it is likely enough that the redundant
      ** xSync() call will be changed to a no-op by the OS anyhow.
      */
      rc = syncJournal(pPager, 0);

header-format.text:
/*
** The journal file must be open when this routine is called. A journal
** header (JOURNAL_HDR_SZ bytes) is written into the journal file at the
** current location.
**
** The format for the journal header is as follows:
** - 8 bytes: Magic identifying journal format.
** - 4 bytes: Number of records in journal, or -1 no-sync mode is on.
** - 4 bytes: Random number used for page hash.
** - 4 bytes: Initial database page count.
** - 4 bytes: Sector size used by the process that wrote this journal.
** - 4 bytes: Database page size.
**
** Followed by (JOURNAL_HDR_SZ - 28) bytes of unused space.

header-write.text:
/* In theory, it is only necessary to write the 28 bytes that the
  ** journal header consumes to the journal file here. Then increment the
  ** Pager.journalOff variable by JOURNAL_HDR_SZ so that the next
  ** record is written to the following sector (leaving a gap in the file
  ** that will be implicitly filled in by the OS).
  **
  ** However it has been discovered that on some systems this pattern can
  ** be significantly slower than contiguously writing data to the file,
  ** even if that means explicitly writing data to the block of
  ** (JOURNAL_HDR_SZ - 28) bytes that will not be used. So that is what
  ** is done.
  **
  ** The loop is required here in case the sector-size is larger than the
  ** database page size. Since the zHeader buffer is only Pager.pageSize
  ** bytes in size, more than one call to sqlite3OsWrite() may be required
  ** to populate the entire journal header sector.
  */
  for(nWrite=0; rc==SQLITE_OK&&nWrite<JOURNAL_HDR_SZ(pPager); nWrite+=nHeader){
    IOTRACE(("JHDR %p %lld %d\n", pPager, pPager->journalHdr, nHeader))
    rc = sqlite3OsWrite(pPager->jfd, zHeader, nHeader, pPager->journalOff);
    assert( pPager->journalHdr <= pPager->journalOff );
    pPager->journalOff += nHeader;
  }

  return rc;

maximum-sector.text:
/*
** The maximum allowed sector size. 64KiB. If the xSectorsize() method
** returns a value larger than this, then MAX_SECTOR_SIZE is used instead.
** This could conceivably cause corruption following a power failure on
** such a system. This is currently an undocumented limit.
*/
#define MAX_SECTOR_SIZE 0x10000
